title: Practice online
hookLine: talks, chanting and sittings now travel by screen

cards: A laptop propped on a stack of books. On the screen, a grid of small windows: a woman by a candle, a man in a parked car, an older monk in a robe, someone whose cat keeps walking across the keyboard.

A bell rings through tinny speakers, and every face in every window closes its eyes at once, in different rooms, in different time zones. Nobody says a word for a long while. Then the bell again, and a few people wave.

teach.b: A dharma talk used to reach the people in the room. Now teachers record their talks, and students listen on a commute or while washing dishes, sometimes years later and continents away.
A hall in Chicago held the speakers we met last week; a phone holds talks from the schools we've met on this road.

Temples and monasteries stream their morning chanting and their services, so someone at a kitchen table can chant the refuges in Pali, or the Heart Sutra, along with a monastery they've never visited.

In the Pali texts, the Buddha's attendant Ananda once said that good friendship, good companions, must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrected him. Not half: good friendship is the whole of the holy life.

That's the Upaddha Sutta, in the Samyutta Nikaya. Online sitting is one way people try to keep that kind of company when a temple is far away, or when they're sick, caring for someone, or can't leave home.

Teachers differ. Some welcome online sittings and teach on screen every week. Others say some things only happen in a shared room: the smell of incense, a teacher noticing your posture, a bow you can actually see.
Some communities do both. The texts don't settle that question. What they do say is that company on the path matters.

how: Buddhist temples and meditation centers stream talks, chanting and group sittings, and practitioners join from home, alongside or instead of sitting in person.

o: reading Buddhist texts alone on a website
sitting and chanting together by screen, far apart
meditation apps that replace a teacher entirely

s: the Buddha told Ananda good friendship is half the holy life
Ananda said half; the Buddha said it is the whole.
Buddhist teachers all agree about sitting online
some welcome it; others say some things only happen in a shared room.
temples stream their chanting so people can join from home
someone at a kitchen table can chant along.

games.q: you're Ananda. you've just told the Buddha that good friendship is half the holy life. how does he answer?
o: he says: not half, the whole.
games.why: in the Upaddha Sutta, the Buddha corrects Ananda: good friendship is the whole of the holy life.

practice: Practice the part that makes a group sitting work, starting and stopping together: when the bell rings, settle at once, without fidgeting into it, and let your breath go at its own pace.
When it rings again, stop where you are, open your eyes, and give a small nod, the way people wave in the grid.

wordCard.voice: Practice online. Talks, chanting and sittings that travel by screen, so people far apart can keep company on the path.

orig.note: Pali kalyanamittata: good friendship, the companionship the Buddha calls the whole of the holy life.

carryVoice: Your line: sitting together, apart. Not half the path: the whole of it. See you tomorrow.
